teaching.causalExplanation: You already know how to find a percentage of an amount. The Medicare levy was two per cent of income, so you multiplied by nought point nought two. A price rise adds a percentage on top. Three per cent more than a hundred and twenty dollars is a hundred per cent of the price, plus three per cent. That's a hundred and three per cent, or one point nought three. So the new price is a hundred and twenty times one point nought three, a hundred and twenty-three dollars sixty. That one number, one point nought three, is called the multiplier. It's the number you multiply by to make the whole change in one step. Up five per cent is times one point nought five. Up fifteen per cent is times one point one five. A decrease works the same way, but you take the percentage away. Twenty per cent off leaves eighty per cent of the price, so the multiplier is nought point eight. A hundred and twenty times nought point eight is ninety-six dollars. A common slip is to multiply by nought point two. That gives twenty-four dollars, which is the discount, the amount you save, not the price you pay. If the question wants the price, use what's left, eighty per cent. Now the sneakers question. Up ten per cent is times one point one, so a hundred and twenty becomes a hundred and thirty-two. Then ten per cent off is times nought point nine. But the ten per cent is now taken from a hundred and thirty-two, so it's thirteen dollars twenty, not twelve. The price ends at a hundred and eighteen dollars eighty. It's not back where it started. Two changes in a row multiply. One point one times nought point nine is nought point nine nine, which is one per cent less. The second change is a percentage of a different amount. And the order doesn't matter. Ten per cent off first, then ten per cent up, also ends at a hundred and eighteen dollars eighty.

scenes.teachingReason: Sometimes you know the two prices and need the percentage. A phone plan goes from forty dollars a month to forty-six. The change is six dollars. As a percentage, compare it with where you started. Six divided by forty, times a hundred, is fifteen per cent. Always divide by the starting amount, the old price. If the plan dropped from forty dollars to thirty-four, that's six dollars on forty, a fifteen per cent decrease. Percentage change equals the change, divided by the starting amount, times a hundred per cent.

scenes.teachingReason: Shops use the same idea for profit. The cost price is what the shop paid for an item, and the selling price is what you pay. Say the shop paid seventy-five dollars for these sneakers, and sells them for a hundred and twenty. The profit is selling price minus cost price, forty-five dollars. Businesses often call these revenue and cost. As a percentage, profit is measured on the cost price, what the shop put in. Unless a question asks for a percentage of the selling price, use the cost price. Forty-five divided by seventy-five is sixty per cent. Why bother with a percentage? Forty-five dollars profit on a seventy-five dollar pair of sneakers is a much better deal than forty-five dollars on a three hundred dollar bike. The percentage lets you compare deals of different sizes fairly. In the sale at ninety-six dollars, the profit is only twenty-one dollars, twenty-eight per cent. Clear them out at sixty dollars, and selling price minus cost price is negative fifteen. That's a loss of fifteen dollars, a twenty per cent loss, still measured on the seventy-five dollars the shop paid.
